query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of germanium (around 2–6 at.%) to a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will trigger the formation of fine precipitates that pin grain boundaries and, as a result, improve the alloy’s elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ti-Ni primary high-entropy alloy without Ge addition (within the conventional 5–35 at% constituents and similar atomic radii)
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor addition of Ge (on the order of 2–6 at.%) into the alloy composition
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposure (e.g., in the range of 700–1000 °C) during mechanical testing such as tensile and creep tests
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine Ge-induced precipitates along with enhanced grain boundary pinning
generation.mechanism: The Ge addition is expected to promote the nucleation of fine precipitates during solidification and/or subsequent heat exposure, which effectively pin grain boundaries and restrict grain growth. This grain refinement and stabilization mechanism reduces dislocation mobility and improves yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unalloyed Ti-Ni HEA, the Ge-doped alloy should exhibit higher yield strength, higher hardness, and improved creep resistance at elevated temperatures.
generation.baseline: The original Ti-Ni primary HEA without any Ge addition
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable provided that the overall alloy composition remains within the high-entropy regime (each element between approximately 5–35 at%) and under operating temperatures up to about 1000 °C, where the fine precipitate mechanism is active.
generation.uncertainty: The exact concentration of Ge for optimal performance and the magnitude of improvement remain uncertain without direct experimental validation. Additionally, interactions with other alloying elements might alter precipitate formation behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the Ti-Ni primary HEA without Ge and another set with an added 2–6 at.% Ge. Process both sets under identical additive manufacturing conditions and perform post-deposition heat treatments as required. Subject the samples to elevated-temperature mechanical tests, such as tensile and creep tests, within the 700–1000 °C range.
measurements: Creep strain rate over a specified time period
Microstructural analysis (grain size and precipitate distribution via SEM/EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ge-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength (e.g., less than a 10% increase), hardness, or reduction in creep strain rate compared to the baseline samples and lack evidence of fine precipitate formation and grain boundary pinning, then the hypothesis should be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of Ge and B improved the protective SiO2 phase grown during high-temperature oxidation and resulted in the formation of a continuous and dense oxide scale []. The addition of 6 at.% Ge in Nb-22Ti-12Si destabilised the Nb3Si, promoted the formation of Nb5Si3, significantly refined the microstructure and improved the high-temperature strength and room temperature fracture toughness respectively by about 88 and 19%, compared with the alloy without Ge []. The fracture toughness (KC, 3–point bend) of as-cast and heat-treated Nb-Ti-Si-Cr-Hf-Ge solid solution and silicide based alloys and the indentation toughness of the solid solution, Laves, and silicide phases have been reported []. The fracture toughness was not significantly changed by heat treatment and was about 10 MPa·m1/2 for alloys with more than 50 vol % silicide and Laves phases while the toughness of the solid solution ranged from 22 to 32 MPa·m1/2.

reading.lever: Add a minor amount of Ge to the Ti–Ni primary HEA to trigger fine precipitate formation and grain boundary pinning.
reading.why: Ge addition has been shown to refine microstructure and improve high-temperature properties in Nb-based systems, suggesting its potential to enhance Ti–Ni primary HEAs.
